newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Bristol-M heart drug succeeds in trial.
newsitem.headline: Bristol-M heart drug succeeds in trial.

text.p: Australia's National Heart Foundation said on Thursday that a seven-year clinical trial of a Bristol-Myers Squibb Co cholestorol-lowering drug will end early this year due to the study's positive findings.

The decision to end the Long Term Intervention with Pravastatin in Ischaemic Disease (LIPID) trial early was made after an independent monitoring committee advised there was a clear advantage of treatment with the drug pravastatin over placebo treatment, the foundation said.
Pravastatin, a cholestorol-lowering drug, was tried on 9,000 Australian and New Zealand men and women with heart disease.
LIPID trial chairman and National Heart Foundation Director of Health, Medical and Scientific Affairs Dr Andrew Tonkin said the trial was significant for a number of reasons.

It was the largest clinical trial ever conducted in Australasia, involving 5,958 Australians, 3,056 New Zealanders and 85 teaching hospitals and was the largest study of its type ever conducted which examined the benefits of cholesterol lowering in patients with coronary heart disease, he said.
As well, each participant's cholesterol level was initially only mildly elevated, average or below average for the general population, Tonkin said in a statement.
"The cholesterol levels of the LIPID trial participants is significant because it represents the majority of patients with heart attack or unstable angina seen in every day practice," Tonkin said.
The trial was conducted under the auspices of the National Heart Foundation of Australia and funded by a grant from Bristol-Myers Squibb, he said.
The results of the study are expected to be presented later this year at a major medical congress, he said.

In a separate statement made in Princeton, New Jersey, and issued here, Bristol-Myers said the early closing of the study represented a milestone in the treatment of most patients with coronary heart disease.

The study was designed to examine the use of pravastatin, a member of a class of drugs called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, in reducing the risk of death from coronary artery disease in patients who have experienced a heart attack or were hospitalised for unstable angina, Bristol-Myers said.
LIPID was the largest trial ever conducted with an HMG and also included the largest number of women, older patients, and patients with diabetes ever evaluated with a drug of this kind.
In addition, LIPID was the first study to examine the use of an HMG in patients with unstable angina, a major risk factor for heart attack, Bristol-Myers said.
With the combined patient populations from LIPID and other major clinical trials, pravastatin has been more extensively studied than any other drug of its kind, it said.
